B Section Works Guide:

1. The Bluebird, Watson Cruz, Children's Literature.
Editor's Review: A children's book, but not just for children. Viewing the world from a different perspective reveals an entirely new reality.

2. Fox Beneath the Sky, Tadeo, Social Literature.
Editor's Review: A classic intellectual autobiography offering profound reflections on the nature of time.

3. Blood Monster, Averroes, Horror Fiction.
Editor's Review: Undoubtedly the finest novel about vampiric creatures this century. A three-hundred-year tale of immortality, jealousy, and humanity.

items.text: The Boundary of Fiction
Expo Guadalajara
1990, Guadalajara, International Book Fair.
People move between bookshelves and corridors, engaged in heated conversations. The air is filled with the mingling of multiple languages.

items.speaker: Editor
items.text: I'm afraid we can't publish your novel in its current state, Recoleta. We look forward to seeing more refined work from you in the future!

items.speaker: Editor
items.text: Ah, Mr. Cruz! What a pleasure to see you here! I'm an editor from Naranja Dulce Publishing House. Could you spare a moment to discuss the copyright for The Bluebird? We're huge fans of your children's literature.
The editor leaves, hurrying after another writer, leaving Recoleta standing alone in place. The 17th publisher to reject her today.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Hey, relax, Recoleta! Look at all the books around you. This place is heaven! You can't get down on yourself, not here!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: There are so many writers and publishers here. It's only natural you'd be turned down 17 times. This is just the beginning!
The young writer, attempting to forget her 17th rejection, flips through the event guide in her hands.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Now, which section should I visit next? Hmm, oh, this brochure might help.
She turns to the last page of the thick handbook, where all the invited authors and their contact details are listed.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Wonderful! An exchange of ideas between writers—nothing could be more incredible than that!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I recall James Joyce was inspired by a letter he received from Henrik Ibsen. So, maybe what I need is to find someone to share my manuscript with, but who?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Tadeo, Emma Zunz, Aleph, Averroes ...
Lima Apartments, Buenos Aires
A knock at the door interrupts her daydream.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, it's you, sir!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Don't worry. I promise I'll catch up on the rent next month! Although I must say, this apartment's hardly worth the price. The cracks on the walls must date back to the last century!

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: Hmph, make all the excuses you want, ingrate. If you don't pay the rent soon, you'll either end up in that crumbling colonial building on the corner or on the street selling oranges at the San Telmo market!

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: By the way, Julia told me you lost your job at that textile factory.

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: You under some kind like "can't work in one place for more than three months" curse or something, little girl?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, you don't even want to know about the terrible things that happened in that factory. All I did was lend the oppressed workers a hand.

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: Bah, you're just like those college kids—full of hot air. Anyway, I'm not here about the rent.

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: Didn't you tell me to watch out for your letters a while back, when you'd just returned from abroad?

items.speaker: Landlord
items.text: Well, here it is, a letter for you.
The girl freezes for a moment, then snatches the letter and slams the door shut, almost buzzing with excitement as she unfolds it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: My goodness! Someone actually wrote back to me! This is incredible! Oh, oh, thank you so much for bringing it to me, sir!
She slits open the long-traveling letter.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: "Dear Ms. Recoleta ..."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It's from—let's see—Aleph!
Street, Buenos Aires

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: Eh, I've been watching you. You're not a local, are you? What are you writing?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, hello! You're right. I just arrived in Buenos Aires three days ago. My trip's been a lot like a Copes tango performance—full of twists and turns, but nothing much worth telling, really.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I'm actually writing a reply to my pen pal! Long story short, I sent him a manuscript of my novel, and to my surprise, he actually wrote back.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Amazing, isn't it?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: In our recent letters, we've been discussing how my novel lacks a key character to drive the story toward a decisive ending.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So we've been debating whether to introduce a new ghost to act as a turning point for the story.

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: Oh, so then you're a writer? Hey, Pancho, come over here! I've found an actual real-life writer!

items.speaker: Young Man
items.text: What's the big deal? I wrote plenty of poems in middle school.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Oh, so you're a poet!

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I have a feeling we're about to embark on an incredible adventure together! Are you interested in joining the visceral realism movement?

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: Vis what? I've never heard of it. But it sounds like fun.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Fabulous! We have no time to waste. Once I finish this letter, you two must join me on a journey to Ushuaia!

items.speaker: Young Man
items.text: Ushuaia? The end of the world? Why the heck would we go to that icebox?

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: Oh, don't be such a downer, Pancho. Just think of the fun we'll have, the breathtaking scenery we'll see, and the incredible stories we'll hear.

items.speaker: Young Man
items.text: Fine, María. I'll deal with the cold if you really wanna go so badly.

items.speaker: Young Woman
items.text: By the way, could you tell us about your novel?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Of course. I'll tell you all about it on the way. Hmm, now where to begin?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Alright, let's start with the cottage with the blue roof in Amalfitano.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: It's been six months since we first exchanged letters.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Since then, I've been traveling. First from Chile to Mexico, then from Mexico to Argentina. And I've never stopped writing.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I'm not really sure what the purpose of my novel is. I just keep writing and writing. I can't stop.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: What power does literature hold? What responsibilities? Perhaps only by continuing to write will I understand one day.
Recoleta flips through her notebook, every turn of the page containing a different-colored letter.
After their long journey, these pages of letters form a faded riddle, their handwriting long since blurred.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Aleph, you're right. I do want an ending to my novel.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But not like this.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: You really have no idea, do you, Recoleta?
Her only reader realizes she has still not grasped what is happening, forcing him to reveal a truth he has long concealed.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: The Rise and Fall of Sanity is your story.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: What do you mean?

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: You are a ghost, wandering this forsaken land, still striving to create a miracle.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: You are a wandering poet born in Amalfitano, the foolishly brave protagonist of the story, and the embodiment of the author herself.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: A reflection, yes. The author, no. You are simply a figment of her imagination, a manifestation of her dream to wander.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Have you not realized it? The literary pursuits and romantic adventures you described ... they are merely faded memories from 1975.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: The poets who joined the visceral realism movement with "you" left Latin America long ago.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Faded memories?

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: As for the novel, it's yours now—a story you're writing, a story about yourself.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: Your departure has turned Amalfitano into a ghost town. The characters have lost their connection to you. They're gradually fading away.

items.speaker: Aleph
items.text: If the novel is destroyed, you too will cease to exist.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Wait, this is ... Ms. Recoleta, is what he said true?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I ... I know you never lie, pen pal.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: In your first letter, you told me that a character's role and fate must be determined from the outset and consistently adhered to throughout the story.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Reading the perspective and insights of a walking encyclopedia—having such a person be willing to share their thoughts at all—was an exhilarating experience.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I had never imagined my novel could develop in this way. Words could hardly describe how I felt in that moment.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: No one but you has ever understood the story of that town, let alone offered any revisions.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Following your advice, I added the Bank Clerk, the Dune Piscator, the Blind Weaver, and the Murdered Donkey Driver.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Amalfitano was no longer an empty town with a single blue-roofed cottage. The new ghostly residents had begun to fill the skies over it.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The story was finally reaching completion. I could feel that the ending was within reach.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I became increasingly eager to meet my pen pal. I couldn't get the thought out of my mind.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I wasn't sure what I would say to this Aleph. A simple "thank you," perhaps? Or maybe a discussion about the future of Amalfitano with its sole reader?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Or maybe I'm no different from everyone else—led up the garden path by "fate."

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: But even if I am a ghost, as you say, an incarnation of someone else, a fictional being—

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So what?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: My resolve will not waver, even if my existence is bound to fade away.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Because this isn't what literature is supposed to be.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You once told me there isn't an ounce of reality in fiction—only voids and glorified lies.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Let me tell you this: whether real or fictional, corporeal or intangible, I have accepted my existence.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Now, let's put a stop to this, Aleph.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: The inmates aren't characters in my novel. They're people trapped in a prison, just as you are.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: By simulating my story here, you have made me into some kind of god, a guilty false creator, a dictator of fate.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I never wanted any of this!
Shattered words and ghostly illusions roar forth, breaking free from the story's structure and the gaps between its lines, filled with regret and obsession.
Torn letters and book pages flutter in the air, like snow in a crystal globe on a winter night.
Everything is quiet.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Ms. Recoleta has vanished.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Did she really "cease to exist" like Aleph said?

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Recoleta ...
